---
title: "Julia Runtime Preparation"
subtitle: "How does the first backend operation obtain a reproducible Julia?"
toc-depth: 2
---

**Status:** the optional-runtime installation boundary is `CONVERGING`.
Existing numerical preparation and process guarantees remain the authority.

## Select dependencies and provide Julia explicitly

The base wheel does not depend on JuliaPkg and does not acquire a Julia runtime.
Install `scnsim[julia]` for the existing Julia-backed features, and provide Julia
`1.12.6` yourself on PATH or through `PYTHON_JULIAPKG_EXE`. In a repository checkout,
`uv sync --locked --extra julia` installs the Python discovery support only.
It does not install Julia. Feature calls ask JuliaPkg to find an already installed
exact-patch executable with installation and upgrades disabled. Missing Python
support or runtime discovery failure raises `RuntimePreparationError` naming the
requested feature, exact version, original cause and installation instructions;
there is no backend fallback. CI provisions the exact Julia explicitly before
backend checks rather than relying on a feature call to acquire it.

Normal Direct, DiagonalRoot, ResponseElement, related sweeps and Optimization
default to same-process JAX CPU in the dev11 candidate and need no Julia.
Explicit `backend="julia"`, HB and Julia-only quantity families require Julia.
`run.explain()` compiler preflight and compiled schematics also need it when
they invoke the native compiler. Authoring, read-only result/resolve/Benchmark
and verified cache reuse do not discover or execute Julia. The base Python 3.12
installation supplies pinned JAX/CMA dependencies; Julia remains optional.
Historical course sources explicitly select Julia to preserve their outputs.

JuliaPkg owns executable discovery only on feature calls. SCNSim does not use
JuliaPkg's managed project as its numerical environment. Once Julia is provided,
SCNSim still instantiates its committed project dependencies as preparation;
this is distinct from acquisition of the Julia executable. Every child process
uses the separate SCNSim-owned project described below.

For a terminal operation, preparation and exact-version verification complete
before request/attempt workspace mutation. The Plan-bound Run workspace may
already exist and remains intact if preparation fails. Failure here raises
`RuntimePreparationError` without an attempt. After Python allocates an
attempt, child-process creation failure and every later transport failure are
attempt-backed `BackendProtocolError` outcomes under the process protocol. The
protocol finalizes the immutable attempt record only after its blocked launch
bootstrap succeeds or fails.

## Ship one internal Julia environment

SCNSim ships these package resources:

```text
src/scnsim/_julia/
  Project.toml
  Manifest.toml
  runtime.json
  src/SCNSimBackend.jl
  bin/scnsim_request.jl
```

`runtime.json` binds Julia `1.12.6` and the versioned algorithm IDs. The first
slice Manifest contains JSON3, CMAEvolutionStrategy.jl `0.2.6` at registry tree
`6bf0985be2c5ea58305d2d04e336684f64fdc12a`, and required standard libraries
only. The HB slice adds JosephsonCircuits `0.5.4` at General-registry tree
`43fa323200866910a93dd06ab8c002ed393ed9bb` (tag commit
`a88bafb8f57ad5b43ef302ae893288f0b75c11e3`). Python locates all resources
through `importlib.resources`, never caller cwd or a user Julia project.

SCNSim ships one internal `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`. The package
launches the JuliaPkg-discovered executable with `--project` pointing to that
internal project and instantiates it when needed. A committed Manifest fixes
the resolved dependency state; Julia's environment guidance
documents that `instantiate` restores the packages recorded by a project and
Manifest ([Pkg environments](https://pkgdocs.julialang.org/v1.10/environments/)).

Semantic runtime identity records:

- SCNSim Python and Julia source-tree hashes;
- the exact Julia version;
- Project and Manifest hashes; and
- the versioned numerical algorithm identity.

A merely compatible version constraint is not enough to resolve an old
receipt.

Python computes this identity from package-owned static runtime metadata,
source manifests, and the committed Project/Manifest before launching Julia.
`resolve()` uses those same installed bytes and never selects, starts, or
queries an executable. The executable subsequently used for a new attempt must
report the declared exact Julia version or preparation fails before numerical
work.

The attempt separately records the actual executable hash, host OS and
architecture, CPU description, Julia threads, BLAS threads, and BLAS vendor.
Those execution resources do not rename the request. Every V1 numerical slice
fixes Julia and BLAS to one thread to reduce avoidable variation, while still
recording the observed values. See
[Catalog and Runtime Identity](catalog-and-runtime-identity.qmd).

The Full V1 runtime supports Linux and macOS. Windows raises
`UnsupportedRuntimePlatformError` before workspace mutation, Julia selection,
or download. The first slice also requires a 64-bit Julia platform so signed
Int64 optimizer seeds can be reinterpreted exactly as UInt64.

## Fail without a hidden fallback

Offline preparation uses only an already installed exact-version Julia and
cached native packages. If either is absent, preparation fails with the missing runtime or
package named. SCNSim does not silently switch environment, edit a user Julia
project, download during `resolve()`, or fall back to an unrecorded system
installation.

Precompilation belongs to environment preparation. Additional custom
precompile workloads are deferred until representative measurements show that
startup cost materially affects the one-process request boundary.
